concept.name: C-trade
concept.definition: The lowest grade in the A/B/C setup taxonomy used in proprietary trading: a marginal or borderline opportunity that technically resembles a playbook setup but lacks confluence, so its historical expectancy does not cover costs. Standard practice is to skip C-trades or trade them only at minimal, exploratory size.
concept.intuition: A C-trade is a trade you take because you are bored or afraid of missing out - the grade exists so you recognize it and pass.
concept.mechanics: Borderline instances of playbook patterns - weak volume, wrong time of day, choppy context - are graded C, which in a disciplined framework means no trade or minimal size. Tracking C-grade outcomes in review typically confirms that skipping them adds to net expectancy by cutting cost bleed.
concept.failure_modes: C-trades are where overtrading and FOMO actually enter the account: each is individually small, but their aggregate cost and negative expectancy erode the edge earned on A and B setups. Grading discipline collapses first on quiet days, when C-setups are most tempting.
concept.misconceptions: Skipping C-trades is not excessive caution - when a pattern's tracked expectancy is below costs, not trading is the profitable decision. A C-grade that wins is still a C-grade.
concept.example: A breakout with no volume confirmation late on a quiet Friday grades C and is passed; its tracked expectancy over similar past instances was negative after costs.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
